name: Taking the Flank
summary: Your army can strike the enemy line head-on, at a flank, or with a feint. Each choice risks a different kind of defeat.

n0.prompt: The enemy holds a line with a left flank, a centre and a right flank. Where do you strike?

options.label: Hit the left flank with your main force
options.why: Flanks are usually weaker than the centre, and a strong blow there can roll up the whole line.

options.label: Attack the centre head-on
options.why: A direct assault is simple, but the centre is where the enemy expects you.

options.label: Feint at the centre, then strike the right flank
options.why: A feint pulls enemy reserves away, but splitting your force risks being beaten in detail.

n1.prompt: Enemy reserves react to your left-flank attack:

branches.label: They reinforce the left in time
branches.why: A fast reserve can stop the flank attack before it breaks through.

branches.label: They are slow and the flank gives way
branches.why: A slow reserve leaves the flank open for your main force to exploit.

n2.prompt: Reinforcements hold the left. Do you keep pushing or pull back?

options.label: Keep pushing against the reinforced flank
options.why: Pushing into a prepared position wastes the surprise you started with.

options.label: Pull back and regroup
options.why: Pulling back keeps your army intact for another attempt.

n3.prompt: The left flank is breaking. Do you exploit the gap?

options.label: Drive through the gap toward the enemy rear
options.why: A breakthrough behind the line can encircle the enemy army.

options.label: Hold the flank and consolidate the ground
options.why: Consolidating secures what you won, but gives the enemy time to regroup.

n4.prompt: The enemy has expected a frontal assault. Their centre is:

branches.label: Strong and well dug in
branches.why: A prepared centre makes a direct attack costly.

branches.label: Worn down after a long fight
branches.why: A worn-out centre can break under a direct assault.

n6.prompt: Your feint draws enemy reserves toward the centre. The right flank is:

branches.label: Left exposed as the reserves move
branches.why: Reserves moved away leave the flank open.

branches.label: Still covered
branches.why: A split force risks being overwhelmed piece by piece.

e1.text: The flank holds. Your attackers are exposed and lose heavily.

e2.text: You regroup. Neither side gains ground, and the enemy watches your next move.

e3.text: The line rolls up. The enemy loses the field and the flank decides the battle.

e4.text: You hold the ground you won, but the enemy escapes to fight another day.

e5.text: The frontal assault fails with heavy losses.

e6.text: The centre gives way and your army takes the field.

e7.text: The right flank falls and the enemy line collapses.

e8.text: Your split force is beaten on the right.

name: Ambush or Open March
summary: A convoy must cross a valley the enemy may be watching. Ambush, march in the open, or scout first, each with its own risk.

n0.prompt: Your convoy must cross a valley the enemy may be watching. What do you do?

options.label: Lay an ambush in the valley
options.why: An ambush can destroy the enemy before they react, if they walk into it.

options.label: March in the open, ready to fight
options.why: An open march is slower, but your force can fight at once if attacked.

options.label: Send scouts ahead first
options.why: Scouts reveal the enemy, at the cost of time and a warning.

n1.prompt: Does the enemy use the valley?

branches.label: Yes, they march straight into the ambush
branches.why: A surprise attack on a marching column is decisive.

branches.label: No, they take another road
branches.why: A wasted ambush costs time, and the enemy may learn you are there.

n3.prompt: The enemy sees your open column. They:

branches.label: Attack at once
branches.why: An attack on an open column can catch you before you are ready.

branches.label: Hold back and watch
branches.why: Holding back avoids battle but shows the enemy your route.

n4.prompt: They attack. Do you fight in the open, or fall back to the fort?

options.label: Fight in the open
options.why: Fighting in the open exposes your force to the whole enemy army.

options.label: Fall back to the fort
options.why: A fort limits your losses, but you give up the road.

n5.prompt: The scouts report that the enemy is:

branches.label: Small and weak
branches.why: Knowing the enemy is weak lets you press forward.

branches.label: Strong and close
branches.why: Knowing the enemy is close lets you avoid a bad fight.

e1.text: The ambush destroys their column and the road is yours.

e2.text: You wait in the valley for nothing and lose days.

e3.text: You reach your goal, but the enemy now knows your route.

e4.text: Your column is caught in the open and scattered.

e5.text: You reach the fort and hold, but the convoy is lost.

e6.text: You cross safely and seize the crossing.

e7.text: You turn back and keep your convoy, but the road is closed.

name: Blockade and Blockade-Runner
summary: A navy blockades a port. The blockade-runner chooses when and how to slip through, and the blockader decides how hard to enforce it.

n0.prompt: You command the blockading navy. How do you enforce the blockade?

options.label: Inspect every ship closely
options.why: Close inspection stops most smuggling but slows all trade and angers neutrals.

options.label: Patrol the approaches and watch for runners
options.why: Patrols are cheap and keep trade moving, but a fast runner can slip past.

options.label: Stay in port and wait for the enemy to run out of supplies
options.why: Waiting costs nothing in ships, but gives the enemy time to find another route.

n1.prompt: A runner tries to get through the closed approaches. It is:

branches.label: Carrying weapons
branches.why: Close inspection catches weapons before they reach the port.

branches.label: Carrying food only
branches.why: Inspecting food ships delays aid and turns neutrals against the blockade.

n3.prompt: A fast runner tries to slip past the patrol at night. It:

branches.label: Is spotted and turned back
branches.why: Patrols deter most runners once they are seen.

branches.label: Gets through in the dark
branches.why: A fast runner in the dark can beat a thin patrol.

n5.prompt: The port is still holding, but the enemy has a second route by land. Do you tighten the blockade or accept the land route?

options.label: Tighten the blockade and move ships to the land route
options.why: Moving ships to cover the land route spreads the navy thin.

options.label: Accept the land route and focus on the port
options.why: Focusing on the port keeps the blockade strong where it matters most.

e1.text: The weapons are found and the port's defences weaken.

e2.text: Aid is delayed and the blockade loses support from neutral states.

e3.text: The patrol holds and the port runs short of supplies.

e4.text: The runner gets through and the port is resupplied.

e5.text: The navy is stretched, and both routes are only partly closed.

e6.text: The port falls to the blockade, and the land route is too slow to matter.

name: Defending a Fortress
summary: You defend a fortress with limited troops. Your layout decides where the attacker can break in.

n0.prompt: You have troops to defend a fortress with two gates. How do you place them?

options.label: Concentrate everyone at the main gate
options.why: A strong main gate is hard to break, but the side gate is open.

options.label: Spread the troops evenly across both gates
options.why: Even cover avoids an easy break-in, but each gate is thinner.

options.label: Keep a reserve and place the rest at the main gate
options.why: A reserve can reinforce whichever gate is attacked.

n1.prompt: The attacker chooses where to strike. They:

branches.label: Hit the side gate
branches.why: The side gate is unguarded, so the attacker gets in.

branches.label: Hit the main gate
branches.why: The strong main gate holds against the attack.

n2.prompt: The attacker chooses where to strike. Each gate is thinly held. They:

branches.label: Hit one gate with everything
branches.why: A concentrated attack can break a thin gate.

branches.label: Make a feint at both gates
branches.why: A feint tests both gates, and the defence holds if it has enough men.

n3.prompt: The attacker strikes the main gate. Your reserve:

branches.label: Arrives in time
branches.why: A timely reserve turns the attack back.

branches.label: Arrives too late
branches.why: A late reserve cannot stop a breach that has already begun.

e1.text: The side gate falls and the attackers take the fortress from behind.

e2.text: The main gate holds and the attackers withdraw.

e3.text: The thin gate breaks under the concentrated attack.

e4.text: Both gates hold, but the garrison is worn out and the siege goes on.

e5.text: The attack is turned back and the fortress holds.

e6.text: The breach is made before the reserve arrives.

name: Guerrilla War: Hit and Run
summary: A small force faces a large army. It can hold towns, strike and withdraw, or negotiate. Local support decides how long it lasts.

n0.prompt: You lead a small force against a large army. What do you do?

options.label: Hold the towns and fight for every position
options.why: Holding towns gives you supply and support, but exposes you to a full attack.

options.label: Strike and withdraw into the hills
options.why: Hit-and-run wears the army down and keeps your force alive.

options.label: Open talks with the government
options.why: Talks can end the fighting, but the government may use them to split your forces.

n1.prompt: The army concentrates against your towns. Local support:

branches.label: Stays with you
branches.why: Support keeps your towns fed and reinforced.

branches.label: Breaks under the pressure
branches.why: Without support your towns cannot hold a full attack.

n3.prompt: The army chases you into the hills. Its morale:

branches.label: Drops with each ambush
branches.why: Repeated losses wear down an army that cannot find you.

branches.label: Holds, as the army keeps its supply lines
branches.why: A supplied army can absorb losses and keep hunting you.

n5.prompt: The government offers terms. Your fighters are:

branches.label: Divided over accepting
branches.why: Divided fighters split the movement and make the talks easy for the government.

branches.label: United in refusing
branches.why: A united movement can keep the pressure on while talks drag on.

e1.text: The towns hold, but the fighting goes on for years without a result.

e2.text: The towns fall one by one and the force is destroyed.

e3.text: The army withdraws, and the government agrees to terms on your conditions.

e4.text: The army keeps its supplies and eventually finds your bases.

e5.text: The government divides the movement, and the talks end the campaign.

e6.text: The talks drag on, and neither side can win outright.

name: Asking for a Raise (Your Manager Responds)
summary: You have had a strong year and want a raise. The manager responds to how you open the talk.

n0.prompt: Your review went well. How do you open the raise talk?

options.label: Ask for a specific figure backed by market data
options.why: A specific, sourced figure anchors the talk where you want it.

options.label: Ask for a reasonable raise and leave the number open
options.why: An open ask invites the manager to name the number, usually a low one.

options.label: Mention a competing job offer
options.why: An outside offer raises the stakes, but only if it is real.

n1.prompt: The manager responds to your figure:

replies.label: Agrees to most of it
replies.why: A figure backed by data is hard to refuse outright.

replies.label: Offers less, with a review in three months
replies.why: A partial offer with a review date is a common middle ground.

replies.label: Says there is no budget this year
replies.why: Some budgets really are frozen, and the talk ends there.

n2.prompt: The manager responds to your open ask:

replies.label: Names a low figure and says take it or leave it
replies.why: A low first number is the most common response to an open ask.

replies.label: Promises a review in six months
replies.why: A promise without a number can stall a raise for a year.

replies.label: Says the budget for raises is fixed
replies.why: Fixed budgets end the talk unless you can change the terms.

n3.prompt: The manager responds to your outside offer:

replies.label: Matches the offer
replies.why: Matching the offer keeps you, which is what your offer was for.

replies.label: Counter-offers with part of it
replies.why: A partial counter gives you more than before but not all you want.

replies.label: Asks you to prove the offer
replies.why: A manager who asks for proof is testing whether the offer is real.

n4.prompt: They offer part of your figure, with a review in three months. What do you do?

options.label: Accept it and wait for the review
options.why: Accepting now secures a raise, even a smaller one.

options.label: Push back with your market data for the rest
options.why: Data gives you a reason to ask for the rest now.

n5.prompt: They name a low figure and say to take it or leave it. What do you do?

options.label: Take it
options.why: Taking it avoids conflict but locks in the low figure.

options.label: Ask for a written review date and a better figure
options.why: A written date stops the raise from drifting.

n6.prompt: They ask you to prove the offer. What do you do?

options.label: Show the offer letter
options.why: A real offer, shown, makes the manager take the threat seriously.

options.label: Back down and say you were only exploring
options.why: Backing down gives up your leverage.

name: Price War: Your Competitor Responds
summary: A rival sells the same product for less. How you respond decides whether it is a price war or a lasting edge.

n0.prompt: A rival lowers its price, and your customers are asking questions. What do you do?

options.label: Cut your price to match
options.why: Matching keeps customers, but it also cuts your margin.

options.label: Keep your price and add a service they lack
options.why: A service the rival does not offer gives customers a reason to stay.

options.label: Keep your price and message your quality
options.why: A quality message helps only if customers already believe it.

n1.prompt: Your rival reacts to your price cut:

replies.label: Keeps its own price, so you both sell at the lower rate
replies.why: Both of you are now at the lower price, and the question is what comes next.

replies.label: Ignores it and you gain customers
replies.why: A rival that does not react hands you the market.

replies.label: Cuts deeper to push you out
replies.why: A deeper cut hurts you both, and the rival may have more cash to spare.

n2.prompt: Your rival reacts to your added service:

replies.label: Copies the service
replies.why: A copied service means you share the market at your old price.

replies.label: Ignores it, and your customers stay
replies.why: A rival that does not copy leaves you the loyal customers.

replies.label: Undercuts your price to win them back
replies.why: Undercutting puts the price war back on the table.

n3.prompt: Your rival reacts to your quality message:

replies.label: Makes the same claim
replies.why: A rival with the same claim makes the message worth less.

replies.label: Says nothing, and you hold your customers
replies.why: Silence from the rival leaves your message unchallenged.

n4.prompt: You are both at the lower price. What now?

options.label: Hold the lower price and cut your costs
options.why: Lower costs keep the margin, even at a lower price.

options.label: Bundle the product with a service they lack
options.why: A bundle gives customers a reason to pay more than the bare price.

n5.prompt: They undercut you again. Do you match the lower price, or step back?

options.label: Match the lower price
options.why: Matching again leaves little margin, and both of you lose money.

options.label: Step back and sell to customers who value the service
options.why: Selling to customers who value service keeps your margin.

name: A Rent Increase (Your Landlord Responds)
summary: Your landlord wants more rent. How you answer shapes what they do next.

n0.prompt: Your landlord emails about a rent increase. How do you reply?

options.label: Say you will pay the new rent if the repairs are fixed first
options.why: Linking rent to repairs gives you something to trade.

options.label: Ask for a smaller increase and a longer lease
options.why: A smaller rise with a longer lease is a usual compromise.

options.label: Say you will leave at the end of the lease
options.why: Threatening to leave works only if moving is cheap for you.

n1.prompt: The landlord responds to your repair condition:

replies.label: Agrees and fixes the repairs
replies.why: Fixing the repairs first keeps the good tenant you are.

replies.label: Refuses and says the increase stands
replies.why: A refusal leaves you with a choice to make.

n2.prompt: The landlord responds to your compromise:

replies.label: Accepts the smaller rise with the longer lease
replies.why: A longer lease gives the landlord security too.

replies.why: A longer lease alone is not a smaller rent.

replies.why: A landlord who wants to keep you will lower the price.

replies.label: Lets you go and advertises the flat

options.why: Starting early gives you the best choice of homes.

options.label: Wait and hope the landlord reduces the rent
options.why: Waiting leaves you with fewer homes and less time.

name: Ceasefire Talks (Your Opponent Responds)
summary: Both sides are tired of fighting. You offer a truce, and the other side answers. The first offer shapes the rest.

n0.prompt: Both sides are exhausted. How do you open the ceasefire talks?

options.label: Offer a short, verifiable truce with a date to review it
options.why: A short truce that can be checked builds trust for the next step.

options.label: Demand that they withdraw first before any truce
options.why: Demanding a withdrawal first sets the price of peace very high.

options.label: Offer a long truce without any checks
options.why: A long truce without checks is easy to offer and easy to break.

n1.prompt: The other side responds to your verifiable truce:

replies.label: Accepts and joins the monitoring
replies.why: Accepting monitoring signals that they want the truce to hold.

replies.label: Accepts but keeps its forces where they are
replies.why: Keeping forces in place is a hedge, but it still allows a pause.

replies.label: Rejects the monitoring as a threat
replies.why: Rejecting monitoring keeps both sides guessing.

n2.prompt: The other side responds to your demand for withdrawal:

replies.label: Refuses to withdraw first
replies.why: Neither side withdraws first, and the talks stall.

replies.label: Agrees to talk about withdrawal in return for a pause
replies.why: A pause in exchange for talks is a small step, but a step.

n3.prompt: The other side responds to your long, unchecked truce:

replies.label: Uses the truce to move its forces
replies.why: An unchecked truce is a chance to reposition, and they take it.

replies.label: Keeps the truce and holds its positions
replies.why: A quiet truce holds, even without checks.

n4.prompt: The truce is monitored. What do you do with the next step?

options.label: Propose a joint review of the front lines
options.why: A joint review turns the truce into a lasting arrangement.

options.label: Keep the truce and wait
options.why: Waiting keeps the peace for now but leaves the cause open.

e3.text: Neither side will withdraw first, and the fighting goes on.

e6.text: The quiet truce holds for a time, but nothing is settled.
